docs.abstract: The Netherlands defied expectations of a prolonged budget crisis on Thursday, rolling out a deal to meet European Union targets.
docs.snippet: The Netherlands defied expectations of a prolonged budget crisis on Thursday, rolling out a deal to meet European Union targets.
docs.lead_paragraph: The Netherlands defied expectations of a prolonged budget crisis on Thursday, rolling out an agreement to meet European Union mandates less than a week after a dispute over austerity measures led to the collapse of Prime Minister Mark Rutte’s government. That collapse opened the door to elections in September that could help decide the future of the euro. Finance Minister Jan Kees de Jager said the budget deal brought the target for reducing the deficit next year to 3 percent of gross domestic product “into sight.” Parliament was expected to debate the measures late into the night Thursday, but with the backing of 77 votes in the 150-seat lower house, the budget put forth by Mr. Rutte, who will serve in a caretaker capacity until elections, appeared certain to go through essentially intact. NOS television, the Dutch state broadcaster, said the deal called for a lower mortgage-interest tax deduction, a freeze on public sector wages and increased “sin taxes,” among other things.

headline.main: The Netherlands: Budget Agreement Meets the European Union’s Targets

docs.abstract: What made Ruth Barcan Marcus more than a great philosopher were her unflinching honesty, unfailing integrity and a will of steel.
docs.snippet: What made Ruth Barcan Marcus more than a great philosopher were her unflinching honesty, unfailing integrity and a will of steel.
docs.lead_paragraph: I first met the renowned Yale professor Ruth Barcan Marcus in the ladies’ room at the Marlboro Music Festival during the summer of 1977. As a music major in Yale College I had taken only a few philosophy courses, and none with Marcus. But word of the arrival in 1973 of the formidable philosopher had reached even the musty practice rooms in the bowels of Harkness Hall; and I had seen her several times, from a safe distance, on campus. Perhaps because this initial encounter occurred on musical rather than philosophical terrain, I managed to ask the woman adjusting her collar in the mirror next to me whether she was Ruth Marcus, “the famous logician.” She laughed and said yes, and then asked what I planned to do with my Yale degree. I told her I wanted to go to graduate school in philosophy, but feared that a major in music, rather than philosophy, would be an obstacle. She replied, “I don’t see why that should stop you.”

headline.main: Woman, Fighter, Philosopher

docs.abstract: A white man who, at his home, shot to death a 22-year-old black man was sentenced to a year in a state detention center and nine years of probation on Thursday.
docs.snippet: A white man who, at his home, shot to death a 22-year-old black man was sentenced to a year in a state detention center and nine years of probation on Thursday.
docs.lead_paragraph: A white man who shot to death a 22-year-old black man who had sneaked into his home to party with the homeowner’s teenaged relative and her younger friend was sentenced to a year in a state detention center and nine years of probation on Thursday, said Hayward Altman, the district attorney for Georgia’s middle judicial circuit. Mr. Altman originally charged the man, Norman Neesmith, 62, with seven offenses, among them murder and false imprisonment. The charges were reduced in a plea bargain. The parents of the dead man, Justin Patterson, believed the shooting in January 2011 and the sentence were racially motivated. Mr. Altman said the case had elements of self-defense and was complicated by the fact that one of the girls was 14, although she told Mr. Patterson and his younger brother, who was also at the house that night, that she was 18.

headline.main: Georgia: One-Year Sentence in Killing

docs.lead_paragraph: There’s a lot of uncertainly surrounding Emily Blunt’s character, Violet, in the new romantic comedy “The Five-Year Engagement,” which opens in theaters today. What’s solid: the monogram necklace she wears in every scene, from her engagement to Tom (played by Jason Segel) to their wedding day. Designed by Suzanne Donegan, the Los Angeles-based jeweler behind the elegant and understated fine jewelry line Mannin, Blunt’s pretty gold pendant is as symbolic as it is stylish. (A newly affianced woman wearing a keepsake that bears what will soon be her maiden name’s initials? One doesn’t need a psychologist to connect those dots.) “The pendant has everlasting value,” Donegan says. “It feels good to wear, emotionally and physically.” Till death do us part.

docs.lead_paragraph: In a private house in a quiet university neighborhood of Kabul, Ogai Amail waited for the phone to ring. Through a plate-glass window, she watched the sinking sun turn the courtyard the color of eggplant. The electricity wasn’t working and the room was unheated, a few floor cushions the only furnishings. Amail tucked her bare feet underneath her and pulled up the collar of her puffy black coat. Her dark hair was tied in a ponytail, and her eyelids were coated in metallic blue powder. In the green glare of the mobile phone’s screen, her face looked wan and worried. When the phone finally bleeped, Amail shrieked with joy and put on the speakerphone. A teenage girl’s voice tumbled into the room. “I’m freezing,” the girl said. Her voice was husky with cold. To make this call, she’d sneaked out of her father’s mud house without her coat.

headline.main: Why Afghan Women Risk Death to Write Poetry

docs.abstract: Madeline Miller retells the “Iliad” from the point of view of Achilles’ inseparable companion, Patroclus.
docs.snippet: Madeline Miller retells the “Iliad” from the point of view of Achilles’ inseparable companion, Patroclus.
docs.lead_paragraph: To the long catalog of odd hybrids that inhabit Greek myth — the half-human, half-equine centaurs, the birdlike Harpies with their human faces, the man-eating Scylla with her doglike nether parts — we may now add Madeline Miller’s first novel, “The Song of Achilles.” In it, Miller has taken on an (appropriately) heroic task: to fashion a modern work of literature out of very ancient stories — specifically, the tale of the Greeks at Troy, one of the oldest and most seminal of all legends in the Western tradition. The idea of recasting the Greek classics began with the ancients themselves; Virgil’s “Aeneid” is, in many ways, both a rewriting of and a commentary on the Homeric epics. More recently, it has challenged ambitious writers like Mary Renault, whose 1958 novel “The King Must Die” brilliantly reimagined the Theseus legend as narrated by the hero himself, and David Malouf, whose terrific 2009 novel “Ransom” invents a moving episode toward the end of the “Iliad.” But in the case of Miller, who earned undergraduate and graduate degrees in classics at Brown, the epic reach exceeds her technical grasp. The result is a book that has the head of a young adult novel, the body of the “Iliad” and the hindquarters of Barbara Cartland.

docs.snippet: Craig Timberg and Daniel Halperin offer warnings on how to fight the spread of AIDS in Africa.
docs.lead_paragraph: In “Partner to the Poor,” the medical anthropologist Paul Farmer writes that “the failure to contemplate social and economic aspects of epidemics stunts our understanding of them.” To this one might add: And hinders our ability to contain and defeat them. Craig Timberg, a journalist for The Washington Post, and Daniel Halperin, an epidemiologist and medical anthropologist at the University of North Carolina, have collaborated on “Tinderbox” precisely to explore these very aspects of the AIDS epidemic in Africa. They set out to identify why AIDS emerged when it did; why Africans were so disproportionally affected; and why some countries have succeeded in reducing infection rates while others have not.

docs.lead_paragraph: When Thomas Bayly was a little boy, snuggled in his housekeeper’s lap, he asked her why she was called Hattie’s Mary. She told him it was her slave name and she’d chosen to keep it “as a way of always having her mother with her.” “Then he asked her what happened to her mother, and she answered that there are some questions you should never ask. You should never ask a prisoner what he did to get put in jail, never ask a widow whether she gets lonely in bed, and never ask a freed slave what happened to her family. Thomas was perhaps 4 when she gave him these answers, and he retained them until he could make sense of them, one by one.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Secular Americans’ worst fears have come true: there is now scientific evidence that evangelical churches brainwash believers. They don’t merely teach that Adam and Eve actually existed and that gay marriage is an abomination. They change the way their members’ brains work. But T. M. Luhrmann, a psychological anthropologist at Stanford, argues that this is not as insidious as it sounds. On the contrary, mental conditioning has a noble lineage in the history of religion, and even (or especially) in this modern age, it can help humans flourish. “When God Talks Back” explains how rational people living in the 21st century can believe that God speaks to them — and why the rest of us should take them ­seriously.

docs.snippet: Laurent Binet’s novel goes inside the assassination of the SS general Reinhard Heydrich.
docs.lead_paragraph: The nameless narrator of “HHhH” has serious misgivings about the novel he is writing. Like Laurent Binet, the book’s French author, he has spent years examining the murder of the SS general Reinhard Heydrich in Prague in 1942 with a view to retelling the story as a thriller. But now he decides it is dishonest to invent descriptions, dialogue, thoughts and feelings on a subject as serious as this. The best he can do, he concludes, is to provide a running commentary on the truth (or otherwise) of what he is writing. “I just hope that, however bright and blinding the veneer of fiction that covers this fabulous story,” he writes, “you will still be able to see through it to the historical reality that lies behind.”

docs.abstract: You have to look closely for the dark edges in the songwriter Carole King’s humble, earnest memoir, which is at No. 11 in its second week on the list.
docs.snippet: You have to look closely for the dark edges in the songwriter Carole King’s humble, earnest memoir, which is at No. 11 in its second week on the list.
docs.lead_paragraph: SONGSTRESS: Carole King’s rock ’n’ roll memoir, “A Natural Woman,” is at No. 11 in its second week on the hardcover nonfiction list. As famous singers go, King has always seemed exceedingly nice — more Janis Ian than Janis Joplin — and her book’s humble granola-and-chardonnay prose is about as earnest as you’d expect from the songwriter behind “You’ve Got a Friend.” But King’s best melodies often have a dark edge, and it’s detectable in her auto­biography too, especially in stories about her four failed marriages. One husband lost his mind to hallucinogens, and another beat her repeatedly before dying of a cocaine overdose. “In hindsight,” King writes, “I probably should have asked Rick these two questions: ‘Why are you living in a van?’ and ‘Are you by any chance psychotic?’ ” The music gossip’s not bad, either. In 1976 King and a boyfriend were watching “Taxi Driver” on the Upper East Side when King ran into Yoko Ono in the movie theater restroom. Ono invited the pair to spend the rest of the evening at the palatial apartment she shared with John Lennon — who had spurned King at their only previous meeting, 11 years earlier. Now she finally had a chance to ask him why. “It’s because I was intimidated,” he said. “No hard feelings, right?” This is Carole King we’re talking about: definitely, no hard feelings.

docs.abstract: Restoration Hardware, the curator-retailer that sells retro-chic furnishings, has also become a collector of vintage architecture.
docs.snippet: Restoration Hardware, the curator-retailer that sells retro-chic furnishings, has also become a collector of vintage architecture.
docs.lead_paragraph: Restoration Hardware, which has forged a successful new identity with retro-chic furnishings, has also become a collector of vintage architecture. Having closed a substantial number of its mall stores in the last 18 months, the company has moved into the Hollywood Regency structure in Los Angeles that formerly housed Williams-Sonoma Home, and set up shop in a 1908 mercantile building in East Hampton, N.Y. Later this year, it will open a new retail space in Boston’s Back Bay neighborhood, restoring an elegant early-1860s building (right) that was constructed for the New England Museum of Natural History (and later housed the high-end retailers Bonwit Teller and Louis Boston). And more buildings will be added to the roster soon. Gary Friedman, Restoration Hardware’s chairman and co-C.E.O., explained that the gracious proportions of older buildings are more in line with the company’s identity: “We think of ourselves not as retailers but as curators.”

headline.main: Past Perfect

docs.lead_paragraph: At the I.C.F.F., the writer and designer Suzanne Trocmé curates British Bone, a selection of china produced by 1882LTD, including Max Lamb’s hand-carved tableware. Now in its second edition, WantedDesign again takes over the Terminal Stores building (28th Street at 11th Avenue), where it will host an exhibition of contemporary Brazilian design and a three-day workshop where design students will make their own light fixtures. In the garment district, the recently opened Moss Bureau (256 West 36th Street, 10th floor) will present “Midway,” a giant, zoetropic Ferris wheel and carousel by the artist and metalsmith Cathy McClure; “Mortal Stillness,” an exhibition of taxidermy by Kelly McCallum, assorted artist-made vessels and Jennifer Trask’s ivory, bone and gilded wood jewelry. And check out the new Standard Hotel East Village (25 Cooper Square), where the Sight Unseen founders (and T contributors), Monica Khemsurov and Jill Singer, will install the work of West Coast designers for the aptly named “Hotel California.” The British designer Tom Dixon will introduce his soon-to-be-available Etch Light Web at London Underground in the basement of the Bleecker Street Theater (45 Bleecker Street). Walk away with a Mirrorball or Jack Light, or order one for home delivery from Fab.com on special iPad stations. And finally, Jamie Gray will introduce the newest pieces of his MatterMade collection, including Meg Callahan’s digitally printed quilts at Matter (405 Broome Street) and at a “secret” location nearby. Happy hunting.

docs.lead_paragraph: How many YouTube hits does it take to get to superstardom? For the musician and artist Arnel Pineda, it took only the right one. When Neal Schon, the guitarist for Journey, was looking for a new singer for the band, he searched on YouTube and found Mr. Pineda, a Filipino singer who was performing Journey songs with his group the Zoo Band. Mr. Schon asked to meet with Mr. Pineda and, eventually, Mr. Pineda, an artist who had logged so many hours impersonating the sounds of rock stars, became one. A new documentary playing this weekend at the Tribeca Film Festival, “Don’t Stop Believin': Everyman’s Journey” looks deeper into the unlikely story of Arnel Pineda and how he became the frontman for one of America’s most popular rock acts. It follows Mr. Pineda on the band’s 2008 tour and spends some time with him in more personal moments as well.

docs.abstract: Batman and his various allies and enemies stay behind when Gotham is evacuated in this story.
docs.snippet: Batman and his various allies and enemies stay behind when Gotham is evacuated in this story.
docs.lead_paragraph: New to the graphic books paperback best-seller list this week is Volume 2 of “Batman: No Man’s Land,” which appears at No. 7. The story was originally published in serialized form in 1999. Those days were hard times for Gotham City and the caped crusader: after an outbreak of disease, the city was leveled by an earthquake. The government had enough and gave the order to evacuate the city. Batman, his allies, his enemies and many residents stayed. The story, which wove through several monthly titles and was handled by several writers and artists, was compelling. The city became divided by rival factions and familiar faces were cast into different roles. (The Penguin, for example, became a supplier of goods on the black market, while the Huntress, who felt ostracized by Batman, took on a new guise.) Most superhero stories require a good helping of suspension of disbelief, and this one is no different. When “No Man’s Land” began, fans wondered why Batman’s heroic allies did not help him or the city. There’s an adventure that addresses that (in a Justice League story, they are shown protecting Gotham’s perimeter, but are asked by Batman to otherwise keep out), which I hope will be featured in a future volume.

headline.main: Graphic Books Best Sellers: A New Volume of ‘Batman: No Man’s Land’

docs.snippet: A new print of Shirley Clarke’s first feature, “The Connection,” preserved by the U.C.L.A. Film & Television Archive, is opening in New York.
docs.lead_paragraph: DANCER, bride, runaway wife, radical filmmaker and pioneer — Shirley Clarke is one of the great undertold stories of American independent cinema. A woman working in a predominantly male world, a white director who turned her camera on black subjects, she was a Park Avenue rich girl who willed herself to become a dancer and a filmmaker, ran away to bohemia, hung out with the Beats and held to her own vision in triumph and defeat. She helped inspire a new film movement and made urgently vibrant work that blurs fiction and nonfiction, only to be marginalized, written out of histories and dismissed as a dilettante. She died in 1997 at 77 and is long overdue for a reappraisal.

headline.main: Woman With a Lens, Restored

docs.abstract: Melissa Clark demonstrates how to make a topping that’s easy, and wonderful to have around, whether you eat it on pancakes, yogurt or just a spoon.
docs.snippet: Melissa Clark demonstrates how to make a topping that’s easy, and wonderful to have around, whether you eat it on pancakes, yogurt or just a spoon.
docs.lead_paragraph: In this week’s column, I mention a homemade rhubarb compote that I used as a topping for pancakes. I demonstrate the recipe in this video if you want a detailed look at how to make it, though it is simple as can be. Just cube 3/4 pound rhubarb and combine it with 3/4 cup sugar over low heat. When the rhubarb starts to soften, but before it falls apart (about 5 minutes), use a slotted spoon to transfer it to a bowl. Then, cook the liquid down in the pan until it thickens and turns syrupy (about 5 minutes longer). This condenses and intensifies the rhubarb flavor. Add the syrup to the bowl with the rhubarb and let cool. It will keep for at least a week in the fridge.

headline.main: Video: Homemade Rhubarb Compote

docs.lead_paragraph: When Alan Gilbert commissioned the composer Marc Neikrug to write a piece for the New York Philharmonic, he couched the request simply: he wanted something that would show off the full orchestra. It could have been a symphony or a tone poem, but for Mr. Neikrug the solution was a concerto for orchestra: a score in the tradition of Bartok’s and Lutoslawski’s similarly titled works, in which every part of the ensemble would be treated equally. His goal, he said in a recent interview on YouTube, was to write music that would require the Philharmonic to “play ferociously difficult music like ferocious animals.”

docs.lead_paragraph: Judging by this week’s debate, you would think that student loans are young people’s only priority. They’re not. Among domestic issues, creating jobs almost always won, while combating climate change almost never did. docs.abstract: The nine things I learned from reading this week’s New Yorker, cover to cover.
docs.snippet: The nine things I learned from reading this week’s New Yorker, cover to cover.
docs.lead_paragraph: Let’s first dispense with the question of whether I really read every one of the 55,000 words in this week’s New Yorker. All I can say is I tried. One of my favorite discoveries was a quote from Walt Frazier. As a girl growing up in New York City, I was obsessed with the Knicks guard. Back then you could write him a worshipful letter, care of the Garden, and get back a signed black-and-white photo. Once before a home game, my friend Paul and I saw him on the street after he got out of his Rolls. We asked him for his autograph — two adoring 12-year-olds offering up a couple of pieces of lined paper — and he told us he was only signing copies of a book about him that recently had been published, and then he turned away. I still loved him. But it was hard not to harbor a grudge. And then came all those years of his jangling play-by-play commentary. But I couldn’t help but feel a new sense of tenderness when he explained himself in Talk of the Town: “When I was a player, I rarely read anything, unless it was about me. Now I get The Times Arts & Leisure section, where they critique the plays: Riveting! Mesmerizing! Provocative! Profound! Dazzling! All these different words. I like the way they sound, so I write them down and use them.”

headline.main: Nine Things I Learned From Reading Every Last Word of The New Yorker

docs.abstract: Everything seems to be regenerating in the spring — every species of plant, animal and insect — all of them cued to the new light and the new warmth.

docs.lead_paragraph: Spring is the torrential season. On a bright, blue-skied day in April or May, it can feel as if you’re standing in a river of biological change, whether you’re in Central Park or out in the country. Everything seems to be regenerating — every species of plant, animal and insect — all of them cued to the new light and the new warmth. It’s as though we’re living in three kinds of time at once: geological time, which is too slow for us to grasp, human time, which is just right, and tulip time, which comes and goes in the blink of an eye.

Before we embarked on the Queen Elizabeth, my brother Philip (age 10) and I took the wise precaution of changing our names. For me it was quite straightforward: I would be known, stateside, as Marty. Philip was more imaginative, adapting one of his middle names and coming up with Nick Jr. — while boldly ignoring the fact that there was no Nick Sr. My middle name, I later realized, would have been perfect just as it was: Louis (my parents were admirers of Louis Armstrong). Anyway, when the great liner approached the glittering immensity of New York, Nick Jr. and Marty were fully prepared.

docs.lead_paragraph: Why has the promise of India remained unfulfilled? Basharat Peer enumerates the many reasons for India’s recent failures and uncertain future in an article in Foreign Affairs magazine. The piece argues that while India’s elite and growing middle class have become increasingly vociferous at expounding their aspiration for India to become a great power, the country has little to show for it. Mr. Peer analyzes two popular books from last year – “Behind the Beautiful Forevers,” by Katherine Boo, and “The Beautiful and the Damned,” by Siddhartha Deb – to show how increasing inequity hampers the promise of India’s growing international influence.

Typed definitions and scientific descriptions of sight, hearing, touch, taste and smell appear on a screen at the beginning of each section; there’s a particular pleasure in finding that there’s no dumbing down in the way information is stated. docs.lead_paragraph: “War Witch,” the director Kim Nguyen’s feature about a kidnapped African girl who becomes a child soldier, was named the best narrative feature at the 2012 Tribeca Film Festival, and its star, Rachel Mwanza, below, was named best actress, the festival’s organizers announced on Thursday night. “Una Noche,” a film by Lucy Mulloy about Cuban teenagers who dream of fleeing Havana for Miami, won the best-actor prize, which was split between two of its leads, Dariel Arrechada and Javier Núñez Florián; Ms. Mulloy was also named best new narrative director for the film, which additionally was cited for best cinematography in a narrative feature film. (Mr. Núñez and another star of the film, Anailín de la Rúa de la Torre, disappeared as they were traveling from Cuba to the festival.) “All In,” Daniel Burman’s film about the romantic life of a professional poker player, won for best screenplay, written by Mr. Burman and Sergio Dubcovsky, and “The World Before Her,” Nisha Pahuja’s film about competitors in the Miss India pageant, took best documentary feature. Two audience awards were announced on Saturday night: “Any Day Now,” the director Travis Fine’s feature inspired by a true story of a gay couple trying to adopt a teenager in Los Angeles during the 1970s, received the audience narrative award, and “Burn,” Tom Putnam and Brenna Sanchez’s film that follows the fire commissioner of Detroit, won the audience documentary award.

docs.abstract: A three-day music and film festival, which opens this week, features work by Janka Nabay, Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Poppy de Villeneuve.
docs.snippet: A three-day music and film festival, which opens this week, features work by Janka Nabay, Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Poppy de Villeneuve.
docs.lead_paragraph: If there are any doubts as to Brooklyn’s status as the coolest borough, Crossing Brooklyn Ferry, a three-day music and film festival named for a poem by the Brooklynite Walt Whitman and curated by the twin brothers Aaron and Bryce Dessner of the much-loved local band The National, should put them to rest. “The independent music scene in Brooklyn is the world capital of that culture,” Bryce says. “And it has a massive visual arts scene.” So when the Brooklyn Academy of Music approached the brothers about putting together a program of musicians and filmmakers who live in the borough, they jumped at the chance. Many of the names on the bill, like St Vincent and the Walkmen, are friends of the Dessners; others, like the Sierre Leone-born Janka Nabay, were chosen to represent Brooklyn’s musical diversity. But despite being organized by a pair of musicians, Crossing Brooklyn Ferry was initially conceived of as a film festival. “BAM is singular in its commitment to commissioning new work, and we wanted the festival to reflect that,” Bryce explains. “Plus it’s exciting for musicians to work with filmmakers, so we decided to commission new films and have scores written for them.” Among the filmmakers who will be screening work at BAM’s Rose Cinemas are Tunde Adebimpe of TV on the Radio, Jonas Mekas, Joseph Gordon-Levitt and Poppy de Villeneuve, whose dreamy, black-and-white depiction of an afternoon on the bayou, “And So, We Begin Again,” an excerpt of which can be seen here, was hypnotically scored by Missy Mazzoli. “Crossing Brooklyn Ferry, the poem, talks about leaving Manhattan and islands,” de Villeneuve says. “I took that as a very literal starting point — I went to the Everglades and then the Ten Thousand Islands.”

headline.main: Borough Haul | Crossing Brooklyn Ferry Festival

docs.abstract: The justices do not want to hear the most versatile of the Anglo-Saxon swear words even when the case before them turns on it.
docs.snippet: The justices do not want to hear the most versatile of the Anglo-Saxon swear words even when the case before them turns on it.
docs.lead_paragraph: WASHINGTON — The most versatile of the classic Anglo-Saxon swear words has, diligent research reveals, made just one appearance in oral arguments before the Supreme Court. The cursing, in 1971, probably won the case, which concerned the prosecution of a vulgar protest against the draft during the Vietnam War. By repeating the word in court, the protester’s lawyer showed that it could have a role in public discourse. Over the next two decades or so, the word was used in nine Supreme Court decisions, typically in quotations of something a criminal had said. Its last appearance was in 1993.

headline.main: A Word Heard Often, Except at the Supreme Court

docs.lead_paragraph: My first New York publishing job was an internship with Spin in the summer of 1987. It wasn’t glamorous. Most of my time was spent in a stockroom stuffing envelopes with T-shirts to be sent to new subscribers. (Perhaps a nonsubscribing friend or two of mine received a Spin T-shirt as well.) I can remember exactly two highlights that summer. First, John Leland, who was a terrific Spin columnist (and who now works here at The Times), took pity on my musical ignorance and gave me a couple of preview cassettes (cassettes!) that would change my worldview: “Sister,” by Sonic Youth, and “You’re Living All Over Me,” by Dinosaur Jr.

docs.lead_paragraph: Christopher Buckley’s satirical novels do not normally prompt cognitive dissonance. But there’s something jolting at work in his latest, “They Eat Puppies, Don’t They?” This book means to be funny, but it’s about China, currently one of the least funny places on earth. It’s not a period piece, but it is badly dated. Much of its charm is derived from a heroine who seems modeled on Ann Coulter. Much of its hilarity comes from contemplating how to kill off the Dalai Lama and what to do with his corpse.
